newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's security council holds first meeting.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's security council holds first meeting.

text.p: Pakistan's newly-formed and controversial Defence and National Security Council held a marathon first meeting on Wednesday, but there was no immediate word on the outcome.
Officials said the meeting, aimed at charting the council's plans, began at about 11.30 a.m. (0530 GMT) at the presidential palace in Islamabad and ended about seven hours later.
Defence Minister Shahid Hamid was quoted by Dawn newspaper as saying the agenda did not include any proposal to declare an emergency, under which a government can suspend fundamental rights.
He also told the newspaper that there was no plan to delay national and provincial elections set for February 3.
The 10-man council, grouping military chiefs and key government ministers, was created by President Farooq Leghari on Monday in a move that has attracted widespread criticism.

Leghari has taken a central role in Pakistani politics since he dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) on November 5 and sacked prime minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
His latest action has generated a fierce row over whether he and the caretaker government have overstepped their powers.

The government seemed isolated in a Senate (upper house of parliament) debate on the issue on Wednesday. Six of seven senators who spoke blasted the council, leaving only the seventh, a government minister, to defend its formation.
The government says the council can give only non-binding advice and its creation has not violated the constitution.
But Bhutto and other critics have accused Leghari of trying to drag the armed forces into politics and acting beyond his constitutional powers in forming the council.

Its military members are the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff committee and the chiefs of the army, navy and air force. It includes the president as chairman, the prime minister and ministers of defence, foreign affairs, interior and finance.
"It attempts to transform our parliamentary system into a presidential system," Senator Aitzaz Ahsan of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party said in Wednesday's debate.
He said that whatever the caretaker government might say, the council was intended to shift the focus of power and the main engine of decision-making outside parliament.
"The idea...is ill-advised and ill-conceived and would result in disastrous consequences," he said.

"There will not be any checks and balances in what the council undertakes as claimed by the caretakers," Senator Khurshid Ahmad of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party said. "It is a supra-constitutional body."
He said he feared the ability of the armed forces to defend Pakistan's borders could be affected by their council role.

Food and Agriculture Minister Shafqat Mehmood, defending Leghari's action, said the council would put democracy on the right track. "The caretakers felt that the ship of the state was floundering and took steps (they) felt were necessary," he said.

The council is empowered to advise on defence and national security issues and on economic and financial policies affecting them. It can also make recommendations on internal security matters and the proclamation of an emergency.
The president may refer any issue to the council without consulting the prime minister.

"We have again been shown that the constitution can be bypassed and vital decisions taken by a handful of people who feel under no compulsion to respect the popular will," Dawn said in an editorial on Wednesday.
